newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE-Labour unrest threatens Colombo port's future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Labour unrest threatens Colombo port's future.

text.p: In the race to remain a regional port, Colombo's port authority is caught between an urgent need to expand its container-handling capacity and labour unions that have threatened to sink a controversial expansion plan.

Port authorities say failure to expand quickly can lead to crippling congestion by the turn of the century, driving shipping firms to ports such as Singapore, Colombo's main rival in the regional trans-shipment business.

At the heart of the dispute between the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) and the labour unions is an SLPA deal with Britain's Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co. (P&O) to expand Colombo port and later build a new one.
"It takes time to build a new port," an SLPA official said. "But time is something we don't have."
CONTAINER VOLUMES RISING

Ports and Shipping Minister Mohamed Ashraff told union leaders in December that the latest projections show container volumes rising well beyond the port's current capacity of 1.6 million containers by 1999.
"Don't give wrong signals that could destroy the port's future," Ashraff said. "We must retain Colombo's hub status. If we lose it, shipping lines will not come here."
SLPA chairman Ranjith Wickremasinghe told union leaders that Colombo had reached 90 percent of its capacity and urgently needed to expand.
"We're fighting with Singapore in the hub port race," he said.
Two big shipping consortia that handled 200,000 containers last year can go elsewhere if Colombo port becomes congested, he said.
TOKEN STRIKE

Unions representing most of the port's 14,000 workers staged a token strike on December 27 to show opposition to the SLPA-P&O deal. They fear the proposed P&O terminal would take business and jobs away from Colombo port.
Ashraff said there would be no fall in SLPA revenue nor will workers be laid off. He promised union leaders he would go ahead with the deal only if it was profitable.

"We're totally opposed to any deal with P&O," said Bala Tampoe, head of the Ceylon Mercantile Union, the biggest port union. "We're not going to allow the port to work normally unless they abandon plans to give it to a foreign operator."

The port announced on January 16 it had sacked 185 temporary dock workers who took part in the strike, and warned of tough action against others. It later converted the termination into a suspension after the workers appealed.
"Any disruption of port operations will have a disastrous impact on our reputation as a reliable hub," the SLPA official said.
The SLPA is holding talks with P&O to turn Queen Elizabeth Quay into a new container terminal to expand capacity, and to later build a new port adjacent to the present one.

The project, estimated to cost up to $1 billion and take 10 years to complete, will see the development of the southern part of the port with at least another six deep-draft berths, for fifth and sixth generation ships. That would boost the port's total capacity to two million containers per year.
Colombo handled 1,356,302 containers in 1996, up 29 percent from the year before, after the entry of new consortia and shipping lines, the SLPA said.
Trans-shipment traffic, which accounts for 70 percent of the port's throughput, rose by 39.6 percent, it said, adding that Colombo port expected to handle 1,550,000 containers this year.
